slides.instruction: Copy the date and LO into your book.
slides.speakerNotes: Opening slide. Children copy the date and the learning objective into their books.

slides.heading: Starter

items: (1)  What fraction of this shape is shaded?  (rectangle split into 4, 3 shaded)
(2)  What fraction of this shape is shaded?  (circle split into 6, 1 shaded)

slides.speakerNotes: Four quick retrieval questions. Children answer in their books. Q1 and Q2 prime the shaded-parts-of-a-whole schema we need for the fraction wall. Q3 and Q4 keep unit fractions of amounts warm.

slides.heading: Starter — Answers
slides.speakerNotes: Answer slide. Children mark their own work in their books.

slides.instruction: Three words we will use today

words.definition: the top number — the parts you have
the bottom number — how many equal parts the whole is split into

slides.speakerNotes: Three vocabulary words. Read each word and definition aloud; children repeat. The visuals on the right support the meaning.

slides.title: My Turn

steps: Shade the first fraction on the fraction wall.
Shade the second fraction on the fraction wall.
If both shadings cover the same amount, the fractions are equivalent.

slides.speakerNotes: I want to know if 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount. I'll use the fraction wall. I shade one half — this much. Now I shade two quarters — this much. Look: the ends line up exactly. Two quarters covers exactly the same as one half. So 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent — they are the same amount, just written differently. That's our first sticky knowledge: equivalent fractions are the same amount written in different ways. Watch this — what if I just added 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom of 1/2? That would give me 2/3. Are 1/2 and 2/3 the same? (Check the wall — no.) So 'add the same to top and bottom' is NOT how equivalence works. Keep that in your head for later.

slides.title: Do 1
slides.instruction: True or false — how do you know?

body.value: True or false:  3/6 and 1/2 are equivalent fractions.

slides.speakerNotes: Cold call two or three children. Wait time. Expected answer: True — both cover the same amount on the fraction wall / both shade half of the whole.

slides.title: My Turn

steps: Write the fraction you're starting with.
Choose a number to multiply by (start with 2).
Multiply the numerator by that number.
Multiply the denominator by the same number.
Check with the fraction wall — both fractions should cover the same amount.

slides.speakerNotes: I want to find a fraction equivalent to 1/3. From the wall I can see 1/3 is this much. The rule: multiply the top and the bottom by the same number. I'll choose ×2. 1 times 2 is 2. 3 times 2 is 6. So 1/3 is equivalent to 2/6. Let me check on the wall — 2/6 shaded… yes, same amount. Now watch: why does this work? When I multiplied the denominator by 2, I cut each third into 2 smaller pieces — so I have sixths. When I multiplied the numerator by 2, I took 2 of those pieces instead of 1. The amount didn't change; I just cut it into more pieces. Name the sticky knowledge with me: to find an equivalent fraction, multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number.

slides.title: Our Turn
slides.instruction: Find a fraction equivalent to 2/5 using ×3

steps: Write the fraction you're starting with.
Choose a number to multiply by (start with 2).
Multiply the numerator by that number.
Multiply the denominator by the same number.
Check with the fraction wall — both fractions should cover the same amount.

slides.speakerNotes: Cold call each step — do not call the keen children first. Guided questions: What fraction are we starting with? What's our first step? What number shall we multiply by? What's 2 times 3? What's 5 times 3? So 2/5 is equivalent to…? How can we check? Watch for: children who multiply only the numerator — the rule hasn't landed; re-model briefly. Watch for: children answering '7/8' (adding 3 to top and bottom instead of multiplying) — this is the addition misconception; stop, show the fraction wall, and check whether 2/5 and 7/8 cover the same amount.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.instruction: Questions 1–3 — recognise equivalence using the fraction wall
questions: Are 1/2 and 3/6 equivalent fractions? Use the fraction wall to help.
Are 1/4 and 2/8 equivalent fractions? Use the fraction wall to help.
Circle the fraction that is equivalent to 1/2:   3/4   2/4   3/6   4/4

steps: Shade the first fraction on the fraction wall.
Shade the second fraction on the fraction wall.
If both shadings cover the same amount, they are equivalent.

slides.speakerNotes: Questions 1–3 are the recognise-phase. Children use the fraction wall to decide whether pairs of fractions are equivalent. Q3 has two correct answers (2/4 and 3/6) — flag this when going through the answers.

slides.title: Your Turn — Answers
questions: Are 1/2 and 3/6 equivalent fractions?   Answer: Yes — both shade the same amount.
Are 1/4 and 2/8 equivalent fractions?   Answer: Yes — both shade the same amount.
Circle the fraction that is equivalent to 1/2:   3/4   2/4 ✓   3/6 ✓   4/4

steps: Shade the first fraction on the fraction wall.
Shade the second fraction on the fraction wall.
If both shadings cover the same amount, they are equivalent.

slides.speakerNotes: Answers to Q1–3. Point out that Q3 had TWO correct answers — 2/4 and 3/6.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.instruction: Questions 4–6 — generate equivalent fractions using the rule
questions: Find a fraction equivalent to 1/4 by multiplying the top and bottom by 2.
Find a fraction equivalent to 3/5 by multiplying the top and bottom by 3.
Jake says 2/3 is equivalent to 4/5 because he added 2 to the top and 2 to the bottom. Is Jake right? Explain.

steps: Write the fraction you're starting with.
Multiply the numerator by that number.
Multiply the denominator by the same number.

slides.speakerNotes: Questions 4–6 are the generate-phase. Q6 is the diagnostic — the addition misconception. If more than a few children say Jake is right, stop and re-model the ×/÷ rule before Apply.

slides.title: Your Turn — Answers
questions: Find a fraction equivalent to 1/4 by multiplying by 2.   Answer: 2/8
Find a fraction equivalent to 3/5 by multiplying by 3.   Answer: 9/15
Jake added 2 to top and bottom. Is Jake right?   Answer: No — you must multiply, not add. 2/3 = 4/6, not 4/5.

steps: Write the fraction you're starting with.
Multiply the numerator by that number.
Multiply the denominator by the same number.

slides.speakerNotes: Answers to Q4–6. Spend extra time on Q6 — it's the diagnostic.

slides.title: Apply
slides.instruction: Find the missing number in each equivalent fraction

criteria.value: The ______ has been multiplied/divided by ___, so the ______ must also be multiplied/divided by ___.

slides.speakerNotes: Three missing-value questions. The first uses ×5, the second ×4, the third ÷2. Q3 is the first time division appears in practice — expect hesitation. If the class stalls, model one before moving on. Sentence stem is available on the right as a writing scaffold.
